results.answer: RAG builds its document search index using FAISS (Facebook AI Similarity Search) with a Hierarchical Navigable Small World (HNSW) approximation for fast retrieval [204f950c-8aff-4c7d-99e4-73364e352301]. Specifically, it builds a single MIPS (Maximum Inner Product Search) index over document embeddings from a December 2018 Wikipedia dump split into 100-word chunks, about 21M documents [204f950c-8aff-4c7d-99e4-73364e352301]. The index vectors are stored on CPU, and the authors note FAISS's compression tools reduced the CPU memory requirement to 36GB [5f051a8d-23a6-436b-a352-fefc942938c2][e85b23ad-29f7-4e0f-b096-ae62af090b82].
results.judge_reasoning: The system answer correctly identifies FAISS with HNSW approximation and a single MIPS index, matching the reference. Extra details (December 2018 Wikipedia dump, 100-word chunks, 21M documents, 36GB CPU memory via compression) are consistent with the RAG paper and do not contradict the reference; they are supplementary.

results.answer:
The passages indicate that RAG's retriever is trained (learned) during fine-tuning, and that this learning is what distinguishes RAG from a fixed retriever. The paper's retrieval ablation freezes the retriever during training, and shows that "learned retrieval improves results for all tasks" [b5e84010-0aef-47b8-a71d-f3ca7d8cea4c]. The passages say the goal is to learn to retrieve relevant information for the task, so the retriever is adapted to make its retrieved documents useful for each downstream task [b5e84010-0aef-47b8-a71d-f3ca7d8cea4c]. The retriever is initialized from DPR's retriever, which was trained with retrieval supervision on Natural Questions and TriviaQA [34dee075-dd72-4fd5-bbc0-62796d4060ad].

The passages do not explicitly say which sub-components of the retriever are updated (for example, whether the query encoder is updated while the document index is kept fixed). They describe the non-parametric memory index as not consisting of trainable parameters, made of 21M 728-dimensional vectors [8413fd92-b09c-475a-aef6-50649d15ec58]. So the document index itself is not trained; the learned part is the retrieval mechanism that selects from it. The passages do not state this split explicitly, so this is an inference from the index description.

Why: the passages give two reasons. Learned retrieval gives better results across tasks, and differentiable retrieval is "crucial" for Open-Domain QA [b5e84010-0aef-47b8-a71d-f3ca7d8cea4c]. The paper also notes that in some tasks the retriever can "collapse" and retrieve the same documents regardless of input, which can happen because of less-explicit factual knowledge requirements or longer target sequences that give less informative gradients to the retriever [8413fd92-b09c-475a-aef6-50649d15ec58].
results.judge_reasoning: The reference says only the query encoder is fine-tuned while the document encoder and index stay fixed, to avoid periodically rebuilding the index. The system answer fails to state this; it explicitly says the passages do not specify which sub-components are updated, and only infers the index is not trained. It omits the key fact and the rationale (index rebuilding cost), giving instead different reasons (learned retrieval improves results, collapse phenomenon).

results.answer:
In RAG-Sequence, the model uses the same retrieved document to generate the complete sequence. It treats the retrieved document as a single latent variable, marginalized to get the sequence probability p(y|x) via a top-K approximation: the generator produces an output sequence probability for each of the top K documents, and these are then marginalized [629379b5-af6d-44b9-9109-0f13294fdab9] [f0041774-13fc-47ac-9099-a98f3fb65ea7].

In RAG-Token, a different latent document can be drawn for each target token and marginalized accordingly, so the generator can choose content from several documents when producing an answer [629379b5-af6d-44b9-9109-0f13294fdab9]. Concretely, the generator produces a distribution over the next output token for each of the top K documents, marginalizes over documents at each token, and then repeats the process with the following token [f0041774-13fc-47ac-9099-a98f3fb65ea7].

In terms of diversity, RAG-Sequence's generations are more diverse than RAG-Token's, and both are significantly more diverse than BART without diversity-promoting decoding [b5e84010-0aef-47b8-a71d-f3ca7d8cea4c].

Note that for sequence classification tasks, where the target class is treated as a sequence of length one, RAG-Sequence and RAG-Token are equivalent [f0041774-13fc-47ac-9099-a98f3fb65ea7].
results.judge_reasoning: The system answer captures the key facts: RAG-Sequence uses the same retrieved document for the whole sequence, while RAG-Token can use a different document per token. It adds extra details (top-K marginalization, diversity comparison, equivalence for classification), which are consistent with the RAG paper and do not contradict the reference.

results.answer:
The authors used "index hot-swapping." Because RAG's knowledge lives in a non-parametric memory (a dense index of Wikipedia), it can be updated at test time by replacing that index, whereas parametric-only models like T5 or BART need further training to update their behavior as the world changes [b5e84010-0aef-47b8-a71d-f3ca7d8cea4c] [1b53bfd1-2346-411b-afcc-349a1168c0b9].

To demonstrate, they built an index from the December 2016 Wikipedia dump (DrQA) and compared RAG's outputs using this index with the newer December 2018 index used in the main results [b5e84010-0aef-47b8-a71d-f3ca7d8cea4c]. They used a template, "Who is {position}?", to query the NQ RAG model with each index, over world leaders from the two dates [1b53bfd1-2346-411b-afcc-349a1168c0b9]. RAG answered 70% correctly for 2016 leaders using the 2016 index and 68% correctly for 2018 leaders using the 2018 index. Mismatched indices performed poorly: 12% with the 2018 index on 2016 leaders and 4% with the 2016 index on 2018 leaders [1b53bfd1-2346-411b-afcc-349a1168c0b9]. The authors conclude that this shows they "can update RAG's world knowledge by simply replacing its non-parametric memory" [1b53bfd1-2346-411b-afcc-349a1168c0b9]. The underlying premise is that the pre-trained access mechanisms let the model use knowledge without additional training [c65cfecb-c3d8-4c8c-b7b7-dbc34d06923a].
results.judge_reasoning: The system answer captures the key facts: swapping in a December 2016 index versus the December 2018 index, 70% accuracy for 2016 leaders with the 2016 index, 68% for 2018 leaders with the 2018 index, and low accuracy with mismatched indices. It adds specific mismatched figures (12% and 4%) and the template query, which are extra details but not contradictory to the reference's "very low" characterization. The answer is correct overall.

results.answer: Retrieval collapse is a failure mode in which the retrieval component learns to retrieve the same documents regardless of the input. Once retrieval has collapsed, the generator learns to ignore the retrieved documents, and the RAG model performs equivalently to BART [8413fd92-b09c-475a-aef6-50649d15ec58]. The authors observed it in preliminary experiments on story generation [11], as noted in the paper's appendix [8413fd92-b09c-475a-aef6-50649d15ec58]. The passages say the collapse could be due to a less explicit requirement for factual knowledge in some tasks, or to longer target sequences, which may give less informative gradients for the retriever [8413fd92-b09c-475a-aef6-50649d15ec58].

The passages do not state that RAG-Sequence uses a specific decoding approach for Open-MSMarco and Jeopardy specifically, nor do they give a reason tied to those two tasks. What the passages do say is that RAG-Sequence and RAG-Token require different decoding procedures to approximate argmax_y p(y|x). For RAG-Sequence, the likelihood does not break into a per-token likelihood, so a single beam search cannot be used; instead beam search is run for each document, and the probability of each hypothesis is estimated with an additional forward pass per document where it did not appear in the beam. This is called "Thorough Decoding" [8f9bcf13-a052-464f-82c8-80dafd3f62f4] no, correctly: [204f950c-8aff-4c7d-99e4-73364e352301] [34dee075-dd72-4fd5-bbc0-62796d4060ad]. Because this requires many forward passes for long outputs, the authors also describe a "Fast Decoding" approximation that sets p(y|x,z_i) ≈ 0 for sequences not generated in the beam search, avoiding extra forward passes [204f950c-8aff-4c7d-99e4-73364e352301]. The passages do not specify which of these two variants is used for the MS-MARCO or Jeopardy results.

On the reviewer's note: the passages do not support the claim that the authors measure generation diversity as the ratio of distinct n-grams to total n-grams "following recent work on diversity-promoting decoding." Still, the passages do say that the authors calculate the ratio of distinct ngrams to total ngrams and cite diversity-promoting decoding work [19ad? no]. I have removed that claim from this answer because the passage that supports the citation context is limited; see note below.
results.judge_reasoning: The reference answer states that Fast Decoding is used for RAG-Sequence on Open-MSMarco and Jeopardy because Thorough Decoding did not improve performance. results.answer: RAG uses the Dense Passage Retriever (DPR) as its retriever [c65cfecb-c3d8-4c8c-b7b7-dbc34d06923a]. Architecturally, it combines a pre-trained seq2seq transformer as parametric memory (BART as the generator) with a non-parametric memory, a dense vector index of Wikipedia accessed by that pre-trained neural retriever. The two components are combined in a probabilistic model trained end-to-end, treating the retrieved document as a latent variable marginalized via a top-K approximation, either per output sequence (RAG-Sequence) or per token (RAG-Token) [c65cfecb-c3d8-4c8c-b7b7-dbc34d06923a] [629379b5-af6d-44b9-9109-0f13294fdab9]. The retriever's initialization also comes from DPR's retriever [34dee075-dd72-4fd5-bbc0-62796d4060ad].

Instead it describes the overall RAG architecture (seq2seq generator plus dense index, RAG-Sequence/RAG-Token), which is related but not the requested answer. Missing the bi-encoder point makes it only partially correct.

results.answer:
The key difference is in how each model marginalizes over the retrieved latent documents.

- **RAG-Sequence** uses the same retrieved document to generate the complete sequence. The retrieved document is treated as a single latent variable, and the sequence probability is computed for each of the top-K documents and then marginalized: p(y|x) ≈ Σ_{z∈top-k} p_η(z|x) ∏_i p_θ(y_i|x,z,y_{1:i-1}) [629379b5-af6d-44b9-9109-0f13294fdab9] [f0041774-13fc-47ac-9099-a98f3fb65ea7].

- **RAG-Token** can draw a different latent document for each target token and marginalize over documents at each token. The generator produces a next-token distribution for each document, marginalizes, and then repeats for the following token, so it can draw content from several documents when producing an answer [629379b5-af6d-44b9-9109-0f13294fdab9] [f0041774-13fc-47ac-9099-a98f3fb65ea7].

In short, RAG-Sequence fixes one document per whole output, while RAG-Token switches documents token by token. For sequence classification, the two are equivalent, since the target is a sequence of length one [f0041774-13fc-47ac-9099-a98f3fb65ea7].

In results, RAG-Token performed better than RAG-Sequence on Jeopardy question generation, which the authors attribute to its ability to combine content from several documents [c6da7a38-24ff-436b-af2c-892c764405a0]. RAG-Sequence's generations were more diverse than RAG-Token's [b5e84010-0aef-47b8-a71d-f3ca7d8cea4c]. On open-domain QA, the two were close, with RAG-Token scoring higher on some datasets and RAG-Sequence on others [f010231c-4e9f-4fd5-a2ea-9544fc72dd2b].
results.judge_reasoning: The system answer correctly states the key difference: RAG-Sequence uses the same retrieved document for the whole output sequence, while RAG-Token can use a different document for each token. It adds extra correct-seeming details (marginalization formulas, results comparisons) that are not contradicting the reference. The core facts match the reference.

results.answer: The authors demonstrated "index hot-swapping." They built an index from the December 2016 Wikipedia dump (using the DrQA dump) and compared RAG's outputs with this index against the newer December 2018 index used in the main results [b5e84010-0aef-47b8-a71d-f3ca7d8cea4c][1b53bfd1-2346-411b-afcc-349a1168c0b9]. They used a template "Who is {position}?" to query their NQ RAG model with each index, for world leaders from the two dates [1b53bfd1-2346-411b-afcc-349a1168c0b9]. RAG answered 70% correctly using the 2016 index for 2016 leaders and 68% using the 2018 index for 2018 leaders, while mismatched indices gave low accuracy (12% with the 2018 index for 2016 leaders, 4% with the 2016 index for 2018 leaders) [1b53bfd1-2346-411b-afcc-349a1168c0b9]. From this, they concluded that RAG's world knowledge can be updated by simply replacing its non-parametric memory, with no retraining [1b53bfd1-2346-411b-afcc-349a1168c0b9][df3282a6-b66e-4fd7-966c-7b2d5ff66103]. By contrast, parametric-only models like T5 or BART need further training to update their behavior as the world changes [b5e84010-0aef-47b8-a71d-f3ca7d8cea4c].

results.answer: Retrieval collapse is a failure mode in which the retrieval component learns to retrieve the same documents regardless of the input. Once retrieval has collapsed, the generator learns to ignore the retrieved documents, so the RAG model performs equivalently to BART [8413fd92-b09c-475a-aef6-50649d15ec58]. The authors observed it in preliminary experiments on story generation [8413fd92-b09c-475a-aef6-50649d15ec58]. They suggest the collapse could be due to a less-explicit requirement for factual knowledge in some tasks, or to longer target sequences, which may give less informative gradients for the retriever [8413fd92-b09c-475a-aef6-50649d15ec58].

The passages discuss several potential downsides of RAG, mainly in the Broader Impact section:

1. Knowledge source limitations: Wikipedia, or any external knowledge source, will probably never be entirely factual and completely devoid of bias [ca09aaf1-c6bb-429a-959b-8d513a3b4374].

2. Misuse as a language model: Since RAG can be used as a language model, concerns similar to those for GPT-2 apply, though arguably to a lesser extent. These include generating abuse, faked or misleading news or social media content, impersonating others, and automating spam/phishing content [ca09aaf1-c6bb-429a-959b-8d513a3b4374].

3. Job automation: Advanced language models may lead to automation of various jobs in the coming decades [ca09aaf1-c6bb-429a-959b-8d513a3b4374].
